#3697. EA is resurrecting a dead commentator with AI for EA Sports FC 27, years after his last appearance in a FIFA game

"He was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back."

EA Sports FC 27 is using gen-AI to digitally recreate the voice of veteran football commentator John Motson - the FIFA video game series' first ever real-world announcer who died in 2023.

John Motson commentated on hundreds of football games over the course of five different decades, starting in the 1970s. The English commentator then became the mainstay voice of EA's dominant football simulation series, beginning with FIFA 96 all the way up until FIFA 2005, when the publisher decided to go in a different direction.

But EA's now decided to digitally resurrect Motson - or, at least, his incredibly recognisable voice - with permission from his family. An update with Motson's voice will go live on 26th November. "There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," senior game designer director Mat Prior said in a statement given to the BBC earlier today.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back," Prior added, explaining that Motson's posthumous role in the game is being handled with a mixture of previously recorded voice lines and AI. EA supposedly went down the AI route since it doesn't have recordings of Motson commentating over newer, more fresh faced footballers.

Fred Motson said it "means an awful lot" to hear his dad's voice in the game again, and he reckons his dad was "always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects," even if he wasn't the most technologically savvy person. EA said it had paid the family for the rights to use Motson's voice and likeness.

Save Our Voices Now founder Peter Caulfield - who campaigns for the government to regulate the use of generative AI voice cloning tech - told the BBC he wasn't comfortable with the project. "In life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed," he said. "Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either." He doesn't have a problem with actors consenting to AI voice replication while they're still alive, however.

A Japanese acting union recently fought back against this very same practice by proposing new guidelines that would stop the replication of dead actors' voices without their permission.

Generative AI has been widely controversial in the games industry for other reasons, too. In recent months, there's been a huge impact on smaller game developers who are worried that their games could be cloned by AI copycats and some who have had to delay their release dates because of Steam's growing approvals backlog.

"The Grounds comes across as a frippery, Ultimate Team rumbles ever on, but FC 27 brings meaningful changes to the fluidity and speed of play. Given that its practical football-game monopoly is more or less unchallenged, EA could do a lot less than this," Josh Wise wrote in Eurogamer's EA Sports FC 27 review.

Grinding Gear Games' Jonathan Rogers urges devs to lead with their best stuff.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every few months, Grinding Gear Games resurfaces with livestreams to showcase all the new toys in the latest updates for Path of Exile 1 and 2. They play out quite differently from your usual game announcements, cutting straight to showing new gameplay features ahead of any preamble.

According to Path of Exile co-game director Jonathan Rogers, this is a key part of Path of Exile's success over the last 13 years. Speaking at games industry conference DevGAMM FTW!, he explained how GGG came up with a winning formula for PoE's seasonal update schedule.

The announcement streams aren't just marketing, he explained, they help dictate what kinds of things the team should focus on with every update. If it doesn't sound exciting enough to rally players around a new league, it doesn't get made.

After a teaser trailer reveals the theme and title of the league a few weeks before the full announcement, the stream dives right into the juiciest details—an approach that Rogers believes is paramount when it comes to selling the update.

Rogers says he's seen some "truly terrible livestreams for game announcements," before slipping in a quick jab: "Blizzard I'm looking at you."

I've watched enough Diablo 4 new season streams to know exactly what he's talking about even if I don't quite agree that it's strictly a bad way to do it. Blizzard typically likes to lead with some introductions before having individual developers break down what's coming in an update.

Admittedly, these can drag on for too long, especially if you don't particularly care about percentage changes to some item or stat. But I appreciate hearing the thought process behind each decision from the people responsible for that aspect of the game. In a time when certain very vocal segments of the audience prefer to think of studios as machines, it's a good way to remind people that real human beings are behind it all.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

That said, I think Rogers' specific point about too many studios wasting everyone's time by holding the best announcements for last is often true. For something like a new update to an ongoing game, everyone is watching to find out why this one is worth logging back in for. I want to see the standout details so I don't feel like I wasted 45 minutes for something I'm not that into.

Sometimes I do like the build-up and eventual payoff for a big reveal, though, like the way Blizzard dropped Diablo 5 at the end of the Diablo portion of this year's BlizzCon or how Larian surprised everyone with Divinity last year. Certain games earn the theatrics. If anything, Rogers' approach just underlines how important it is for studios to read the room and craft their announcements around the things that will actually spark interest rather than putting everyone to sleep.

#3694. Original Devil May Cry and Bayonetta director Hideki Kamiya really wants Konami to let him make a "truly insane" Castlevania game

Action game maestro Hideki Kamiya really wants to make a new Castlevania game with publisher Konami.

The long-time developer best known for his work in the director's chair on a host of beloved games - Bayonetta, Resident Evil 2, Okami, Devil May Cry and The Wonderful 101 included - recently published a new video to his personal YouTube account. While the video was first recorded last year, it does give us some hints on what Kamiya is interested in making after his in-development Okami sequel wraps up.

Perhaps the most noteworthy tidbit came from Kamiya advocating to make a new game in Konami's vampiric action-adventure series. "We'll definitely make Castlevania. If you let us work on it, we can make something truly insane, so just contact us and we'll be at your service," Kamiya said. (Thanks, Automaton!)

Kamiya presumably has his hands full with Capcom's Okami 2, which is currently in production at the director's newfound independent studio Clovers. Needless to say, any potential Kamiya-led Castlevania game will likely need to wait in a coffin for a while more.

In the meantime, it's not like Castlevania has remained dormant and defanged. Earlier this year, Konami promised that "numerous new products around Castlevania" are in the pipeline. While new games weren't explicitly confirmed, it's safe to assume Konami would be interested in hearing pitches from outside devs. Kamiya can stay hopeful knowing that Evil Empire just dropped another gorgeous, aggressive action-platformer in the series.

"Like Rose herself, the game is earnest, intelligent, and capable of brilliance. But, mimicking its protagonist, it is also awkward, and unable to fully come to terms with its own unique identity in the shadow of its over-bearing legacy," Dom wrote in Eurogamer's Castlevania: Belmont's Curse review. "By no means is Belmont's Curse a bad game, I just think Evil Empire sunk its teeth a bit too deep into something it wasn't quite ready to consume."

This isn't the first time Kamiya has publicly expressed interest in reviving older games, either. He recently said he's "100% serious" about bringing back Scalebound, his cancelled Xbox One exclusive.

The Xbox One had a reasonably strong launch lineup that included juggernauts like Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag and Battlefield 4 launching right alongside the hardware in 2013, but it was originally supposed to have some extremely strong RPG representation in Dragon Age: Inquisition. Well, that's what BioWare told EA, anyway.

Talking to Pembridge TV (timestamp), former Dragon Age series lead and longtime BioWare veteran Mark Darrah says the studio straight-up fibbed when it told EA Inquisition would be a launch day title for the Xbox One generation of consoles.

"The pitch for Dragon Age: Inquisition was that it was going to be a launch title for the Xbox 360, so it was basically supposed to come out in 2013," Darrah says, before realizing he got his generations mixed up and was really thinking of Xbox One. That console, alongside the PS4, launched in November 2013, while Dragon Age: Inquisition didn't release until about a full year later in November 2014. "It was literally supposed to be a launch title for the Xbox One."

Presumably, Darrah is using Xbox One as shorthand for the eighth generation of consoles, because Dragon Age: Inquisition released in tandem on PS4 and Xbox One. That means EA was likely under the impression that the game would be a PS4 launch title as well, which of course didn't happen, and according to Darrah, that was never even the real plan at BioWare.

"To be clear, we were lying," says Darrah. "It was never gonna happen, and we didn't even build around – like, we didn't pretend and make the team work to that date. We just lied.

"To be honest, Dragon Age: Inquisition got made in large part because they were really happy with Dragon Age 2, and the game was supposed to come out in two-and-a-half years, that seems good, and so they basically were on board, and then we moved it a year, and then we moved it six weeks."

Naturally, EA probably wasn't too happy about BioWare's switcharoo, but I'm guessing it was more than happy to forgive the studio when Dragon Age: Inquisition became BioWare's best-selling single game at 12 million units sold, a massive overperformance from EA's expectations. Tragically, that would mark a high point as well as a turning point for BioWare, with things largely going downhill from there with Mass Effect: Andromeda, Anthem, and finally Dragon Age: The Veilguard being the commercial nail in the coffin for the studio, which was shut down by EA in October.

Though Vermintide 2's had a Steam Workshop since 2018, it's mostly used for quality-of-life stuff like UI tweaks. That's set to change now that Fatshark has announced a public release of its internal developer tools, which they say "will allow modders to work their magic on both editing and creating anything from custom levels, models, textures, particles, animations, and more!"

Right now, only a select number of sanctioned mods can be used in Vermintide 2's "official realm" which is the one with loot and leveling that carries over, while unsanctioned mods can only be accessed in a "modded realm" where there are no progression systems. Obviously that's off-putting to a lot of players, so Fatshark has announced a change.

"We have an update releasing in early December which will see the Modded Realm have its own, local, offline progression. That means that playing in the Modded Realm will still result in you gaining loot and experience, but said progression will not reflect on the Official Realm. This should make playing on the Modded Realm feel much better and not be discouraging for those that want to try out all of the unsanctioned mods, both the ones that already exist and the ones to come thanks to the Mod Tools!"

I'm not sure how many players will be happy to start over from level one just to get access to a wider variety of mods, but I hope it encourages some folks to check them out. Another thing that'll encourage new players is that XP has been doubled from now through till Monday, and Vermintide 2 is on sale for 90% off on Steam. The DLC has been discounted too.

In less good news, the servers for Versus Mode are being turned off. "We have monitored the use of the dedicated Versus servers lately," Fatshark said, "and come to the conclusion that they are barely used. We have therefore decided to shut these down." Versus Mode will still be playable, but via the menu option for a custom game or the lobby browser. You'll have to find a crew to play with on Discord first, which is how everyone seems to play Versus at the moment anyway.

That shutdown is planned for early December, at the same time as the update that adds local progression to the modded realm. That update will also include balance changes to buff some unpopular talents, new weapon icons, and a Tome of Triumphs in the hub area that will point you at any event if there's a live one, or to the weekly event mode if there isn't. The next event planned is the annual return of Gifts of the Wolf Father in December.

Finally, Fatshark mentioned that focusing on the mod tools to get them ready for public release had to take priority from other updates. "The weapon pack and the level that we mentioned in the past has been put on hold," they wrote. "We still want to get back to that, especially the weapon pack, but for now there is no active development on that. It’s important for us that we have transparency here, and while we are not working on these things, we do stick with our games! We have plans both near and far for Vermintide 2."

#3691. US Forest Service Releases Bigfoot Reports That Read Like Something Out Of Control

One of my favorite video games is Control. I also like this year’s Control Resonant, but not quite as much. And one of the best parts of those games is the government reports and files documenting creepy happenings and events in the game’s universe. Meanwhile, here in real life, the United States Forest Service has recently released some files about Bigfoot, and I was very pleased to see that feel like they fell right out of Control.

As reported by The New York Times, last month the USFS published a few documents and reports related to Bigfoot as part of a Freedom of Information request. One file is just a clipping of a newspaper article from a Montana newspaper in the ’80s about big, strange footprints found in the snow. The other two are far more interesting.

First, a 1982 report written by someone who was sent out to study alleged Bigfoot tracks found in Mill Creek, Oregon. Look at this and tell me it doesn’t look and read like something you’d pick up in Control.

The report goes over, in a lot of detail, the footprints that were spotted. Ultimately, the report’s conclusion was that these tracks were fake, with the writer citing inconsistencies with gait pattern, signs of tampering with leaves, and other pieces of evidence that led them to conclude the tracks were “made by something other than a 300-pound plus two-footed being.”

The other piece of Bigfoot documentation released by the USFS is what appears to be a short document written by someone who really thought Petty Creek, Montana was special and historically important. One reason it was historically important: Bigfoot, baby. Here’s the bit about a Bigfoot sighting that allegedly happened in the ’40s.

Another type creature that walked on its hind legs, that altho there wasn’t actual sightings, tracks, a strong odor, and a grunting sound were observed. The first time was when four of us went in to pack out a six point bull elk on our backs and on arriving where the elk was supposed to be laying we found the intrails only and in the snow coming to and leading away from the area was a large set of tracks. At first we guessed it was a very large bear except bears don’t walk on their hind legs only for short distances and ordinarily would drag a carcass this large.

Whatever it was had picked up the elk whole and clear of the ground. We started following the tracks and after about one half mile said creature had stepped across a 3 ft. diameter log that was laying on the ground and on top of the log in the snow we could see where the horns had drug. At this point we held a con- ference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was and tho we didn’t confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs.

This event took place in 1949 in the South fork of Petty cr. about where the present Garden point road goes. The following year when W.W. Schmitz was hunting in the upper Bills creek area he came across the same type of tracks and smelled a strong odor and heard a grunting type noise. He decided that he could find elk elsewhere and left the area. At this time we had never heard of Bigfoot so passed it off as something we didn’t want anything to do with and let it go at that.

The whole thing was typed up on a typewriter and even contains a bit of extra text at the bottom, written afterwards by hand. All of this, including the official seals, the black-and-white photos, and the matter-of-fact writing in the official report, feels like stuff I’d read in Control right before encountering Bigfoot. Sadly, it’s unlikely a big ape stalks the woods of the United States. But it’s fun to read about it, you know?

#3690. The Fable reboot had to look beyond Lionhead's RPG trilogy because games like The Witcher 3 "became the gold standard"

Developer Playground Games had to look beyond Lionhead's original run of Fable games when rebooting the classic fantasy series, and it's all thanks to games like The Witcher 3, which changed what many players expect from their big RPGs and set a new "gold standard."

The upcoming Fable reboot is finally ending its decade-long development journey soon. Playground Games had to set up an entirely new team to work on its fairytale revival, so Fable's production wasn't quite as smooth sailing as the studio's consistently excellent Forza Horizon series, for example.

Asked about what's changed during that time, in an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, studio founder and general manager Ralph Fulton named technological advancements as a biggie, but the impact of other games was perhaps even greater.

"In 2015, The Witcher 3 redefined what an open-world action RPG looks like and became the gold standard," Fulton said. "And after that bar was raised, the Assassin's Creed franchise changed into this more modern iteration with Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla, and became like a quasi-RPG."

"All of these games continue to reset player expectations," he continued. Millions of players suddenly had certain expectations about what their big-budget, open-world role-playing games should look like. So, Playground couldn't pull inspiration from Fable and Fable alone.

"I think looking only to the original Fable trilogy for inspiration would leave us lacking in terms of what the modern audience, the modern marketplace, expects," Fulton added.

Still, Playground's Fable is drawing most heavily from Lionhead's Fable. Fulton specifically mentions the game's signature British wit and in-flux morality system as examples. Then there's also the spontaneous life sim elements that "none of our competitors do," according to Fulton. "It's a totally Fable thing, the social simulation and economic simulation. Okay, there are games that have economic simulations, but they're not in [our] RPG category. Fable is unique in that it's almost like a life sim in terms of genre."

Raising four separate families and becoming the entire map's benevolent landlord was one of the funnest parts of Fable back in the day, alongside those sometimes silly characters. Seeing next year's Fable lean into those systemic choices, and having Albion's NPCs react to them more believably, could give this one a very long shelf life.

One thing I think that’s really underrated about Hallmark is how the network’s projects manage to do a lot without the world’s largest budgets. (These aren't upcoming MCU movies!) Sometimes, however, a little bit of good karma wafts a production’s way just like a snowflake in the crisp winter air. This is exactly what happened on the set of Mistletoe Murders when the show found Fletcher’s Grove, the cool small town hide out Emily Lane (Sarah Drew) opens her Christmas shop in. Apparently, the show has Reacher to thank for this.

While Reacher is not known for having the insane budgets some of Amazon Prime Videos other shows like Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power have had, the show did once create an entire facade for a small town and then left it behind after less than a month.

If you’ve seen Reacher, you know the set. It’s on the Pickering Backlot in Ontario, and it was used during Season 1 to create Margrave, the fictional Georgia town that sees Jack Reacher facing the death of his brother and getting accused of murder himself. It’s a great season of TV, and it came with a pretty nice set, so nice that when Mistletoe Murders was scouting around, they thought it would be the perfect setting for Fletcher’s Grove.

Hallmark brought CinemaBlend to the set of Mistletoe Murders, where producer Michelle Melanson told me what happened, and how they fortuitously came across the former Reacher property.

I believe they used it for 18 shoot days. That’s it. And then they left it. It’s on land owned by the city of Pickering, but William F. White at Sunbelt said, ‘Well we can maybe use this, we can rent it to productions.’ So, that’s what they did, they sort of rented it to productions. And when we saw it – it’s a little small town – we were like, ‘This is Fletcher’s Grove.’

To Amazon’s credit, there’s a little more to it than just having an excess of money to build a whole city and dump it. Season 1 of Reacher was originally expected to film in Georgia. Then, the pandemic hit and plans changed. It was easier and safer to build a little town on a spot in the middle of nowhere in Canada, and that’s exactly what the show did.

Now, it’s a bit of “backlot trivia” in Mistletoe Murders’ own story, though the Hallmark series also has its own indoor set, which helps them to control temperature while filming during hot summers. It also gives them the ability to move forward should Amazon ever want to tear down the “real” Margrave/Fletcher’s Grove.

So that’s our little backlot trivia. We dress it up. That’s where the Mistletoe is. This year we’re excited; we have things like a Christmas market. We wanted to save ourselves because this backlot could go away at any time. They could decide they don’t want to keep it; so we built this set.

I love it when two shows I deeply enjoy have synergy like this. Prior to being able to visit the set of Mistletoe Murders ahead of this fall's Season 3 return on the 2026 TV schedule, I would never have known the Sarah Drew-led series would have anything in common with the Alan Ritchson series, but this is one very cool connection.

Jessica Rawden is Managing Editor at CinemaBlend. She’s been kicking out news stories since 2007 and joined the full-time staff in 2014. She oversees news content, hiring and training for the site, and her areas of expertise include theme parks, rom-coms, Hallmark (particularly Christmas movie season), reality TV, celebrity interviews and primetime. She loves a good animated movie. Jessica has a Masters in Library Science degree from Indiana University, and used to be found behind a reference desk most definitely not shushing people. She now uses those skills in researching and tracking down information in very different ways.

In its latest update on deprecated features in Windows, Microsoft casually mentioned that "Telnet Client is deprecated and will be removed from Windows in a future release."

This may not mean much to you if you didn't do a lot of computer networking in the 1990s or earlier, but the text-based protocol for remotely opening command-line interfaces was a workhorse we used for a bunch of things. It's how antique university lab computers that didn't even have Netscape Navigator installed connected to the internet, how I played text-based online games like the Discworld MUD back in the day, and how we used to connect to our routers.

By default, Telnet didn't encrypt all the data it was swapping back and forth between computers, which is why it's since been replaced by tools like SSH and PowerShell. So it's not a surprise that it's being deprecated, and honestly I'm impressed that it outlived both WordPad and Cortana.

A Windows feature being deprecated means that it won't be in active development and is a candidate for removal in a future update, so Telnet isn't being 86ed immediately. If you're still using it to test network connections because that's what you're used to then carry on as you were, but get ready to grumble and switch over to PowerShell when Microsoft finally does pull the plug.

#3687. With Grand Theft Auto 6, The Series Has Outgrown Some Of Its Joke Brand Names

One thing that keeps striking me about Grand Theft Auto 6 is how good the writing is, even compared to that in previous games in the series. I enjoyed those earlier games, sure, but the dialogue and storytelling in GTA 6 are a cut above the rest in terms of both the game’s compelling characters and its worldbuilding. The fact that GTAÂ is set in an analogue of the real world helps the worldbuilding bridge gaps that most fictional universes couldnât, but Iâm increasingly finding that the standout writing is fighting a war within the game itself against some of the other jokes that have been building up in the series for over a quarter century.

Grand Theft Auto, for obvious reasons, canât use the existing brand names that we see every day in real life. In this sense it’s the opposite of the Like a Dragon series, which proudly wears all its licensed brand deals on its chest and even had to write a narrative around losing the license to a key landmark in the seventh game in the series. Talking Budweiser into lending their brand name to GTA 4 would have been an uphill battle and maybe also raised some uncomfortable questions about the gameâs proximity to real-world places and events. Better to just call your in-game equivalent Pisswasser and move on.

But weâre in 2026 now. The writing in theÂ GTA games has elevated and, to Rockstarâs credit, so have the fake brand names in general. Taco Bomb is a pretty good one as a stand-in for Taco Bell. ZIP for GAP is also good. Weazel News for Fox News makes sense on a couple of different levels, Snapmatic for Instagram is something that you recognize immediately upon hearing it. But there are a handful of brand names I think the series needs to ditch, as theyâre taking away from the more interesting narratives Rockstar wants to tell.

Pisswasser is not a bad joke on its own, but it wears its welcome out fast. Marbles, the McDonaldâs stand-in in GTA, sells a burger called Big Balls. I get it, Big Mac, Big Balls, sure. But come on, man. Weâre scraping the bottom of the barrel here. Zombix isnât even a good pun. Itâs like someone filed that one in the ten minutes before the deadline. We need to start thinking intelligently about which of these benefit worldbuilding and which detract from it.

I’m not saying all of these need to go or even a majority of them. There are plenty of good joke brand names, but there are also ones that are very, very 2000s, and it would be better for the games if they disappear. Grand Theft Auto has grown with its audience, and it’s now delivering narratives that genuinely keep up with well-written modern movies, so why are we limiting aspects of it to jokes that would appear in an Epic Movie parody?

Rockstar can and should start taking a look at these and see what makes sense for their games every so often. Audit the world, donât just assume that because it existed in previous games, it needs to exist forever.

Itâs not like brands donât just disappear from the real world all the time. Joannâs Fabrics isnât around anymore, but your world keeps spinning, just like it would if the Obey car line simply did not appear in a new game. You planning to take a Spirit Airlines flight this holiday? Youâre sure as hell not, nor would you be a sobbing mess on the floor if a Big Balls sandwich billboard wasnât overlooking a highway chase.

There are already so many good jokes in these games that the lame ones can get cut out without losing anything. No one is wrong for liking them, but maybe the games themselves can be better for examining what works and what doesnât. No series has ever escaped a need for refreshing itself and iterating over the years and, in almost every way, GTA 6 nails it. Thereâs just one more thing I want to see them look at before they build their next GTA world, asking themselves if each jokey brand name still fits their vision. If it does, great! If they decide it would be better to snip, that would be fine, too.

#3686. GTA 6 reinvigorates PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S/X console sales in the US, even at their inflated prices

Despite the far higher prices of PlayStation and Xbox consoles today compared to their launch, or even the same period last year, both brands of console saw a significant boost in US sales leading up to the launch of this generation's biggest game: Grand Theft Auto 6.

In the week ending 14th November, PS5 hardware unit sales registered a 2.4x increase over the same week last year. Xbox wasn't far behind, seeing a 2.3x increase in its own unit sales. That's according to industry analyst Mat Piscatella at Circana, who pulled the data from Circana's retail tracking service, which covers the US retail market.

The PS5 Pro only accounted for less than 10 percent of the PlayStation's total unit sales, by the way, which Piscatella noted was "a LOT better than it has been in recent weeks", and seemingly the result of increased supply.

GTA 6, of course, released on 19th November, so the surge in console hardware sales was clearly driven by the rush to attain consoles before the game came out. And while the GTA 6-driven demand isn't surprising, it's worth noting how much more expensive PS5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles are today.

A standard PS5 today costs $650, compared to $550 a year ago. The PS5 Pro saw a big jump from $750 last November to $900 today. The base Xbox Series X jumped from $650 last year to $800 today, while Series S now costs $500, up from $400.

Even Switch 2, where GTA 6 is not available, saw a notable boost of 40 percent in hardware sales over the same period, driven by The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and the special edition Zelda Switch 2 console.

Circana's November US video game market report, which releases in December, is already one of the most anticipated this year, for digesting and documenting the GTA 6 effect. Worldwide, GTA 6 sold more than 32.5m copies in one day, making Rockstar's parent company Take-Two $3.79bn (£2.89bn) in revenue. We haven't had any updated official sales figures since; but estimates suggest the sales figure could be well into the 40-millions. Perhaps Rockstar is waiting to hit the nice round 50m sales mark before announcing it.

"I am supporting all those people that have work to do"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's often a tragic backstory to any great game in which developers were forced to work way beyond their scheduled hours, often late into nights and even on weekends. Usually, the perception is that everyone's working their tail off to get a project out the door in time for whatever deadline is set by the publisher, but in the case of BioWare's seminal 2003 RPG Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, a lot of people showed up at the studio just because they felt bad for people who actually had stuff to do.

John Winski, a former employee of BioWare going all the way back to 1996, reflects on Knights of the Old Republic's development in a recent conversation with Pembridge TV. "I think we worked five months of crunch time," he says. "We started with Tuesdays and Thursdays, we'd work 12-hour days. Then it became five days a week working 12-hour days. Saturdays, I don't know how long we were doing seven days a week, 12-hour days."

That's a lot of crunch. Without official numbers to go by, it's hard to know how that stacks up against notoriously crunch-heavy development cycles like The Last of Us 2, Red Dead Redemption 2, and Cyberpunk 2077, but if you're doing the math, that equates to 84-hour work weeks, more than double the average in most places. According to Winski, "a lot of times it was sympathy crunch," meaning workers who weren't required to come into the studio were doing so anyway because they felt bad for those dealing with mandated crunch.

"You don't have any work, but a bunch of other people have to be here, so you're gonna be here too. Which wasn't great, but also, if you look back, it's like, 'I am supporting all those people that have work to do," adds Winski. "Why wouldn't I be? And when you're young, you're kind of stupid and going, 'well, let's just do it', and it worked."

Can't argue with that. I mean, I'll argue all day long against crunch culture, but there's no denying that Knights of the Old Republic was a huge success, becoming an immediate hit and the best-selling Star Wars game of all time when it released. It's also not just one of the best Star Wars games to this day, it's also one of the most beloved RPGs of all time, proving that, unfortunately, great games can come from problematic working environments.

On the other hand, I'm reminded of comments from earlier this year made by Fallout co-creator Tim Cain, who offered a different perspective on crunch in the games industry. While he said he's "glad things have changed" and called Fallout's development "unsustainable," Cain said the developers working unreasonable hours on Fallout were doing so because "they loved what [they] were doing." I'd like to think the Knights of the Old Republic team felt the same.

SNL surprised fans earlier this season with a David S Pumpkins sketch to celebrate the off-beat spooky character’s tenth anniversary. Current cast member Mikey Day was joined by his OG co-stars Tom Hanks and Bobby Moynihan for what hilariously turned out to be several minutes of freezing in place while James Austin Johnson paused the sketch for his President Trump impression. The bit went over very well with fans at home, but it turns out the broadcast version contained a key change suggested by Tom Hanks who was looking out for everyone’s bodies.

During the original version, Hanks, Moynihan and Day all apparently froze in really exaggerated and over the top poses. Unfortunately for them, they didn’t realize that Johnson’s part with Trump was going to go on for so long. He ultimately talked for four minutes, which left the Pumpkins trio gassed by the time they had to unfreeze and act again. So, Hanks suggested they make a change before the live show.

Here’s how Moynihan described the conversation he had with Hanks after dress rehearsal to Mashable…

In between dress and air, Tom came over to me and was like, ‘Hey, so, we’re all going to close our mouths.’ We were all doing our poses for dress, and on air, we’re just (standing there with our arms folded). We knew we had to stand there for the whole sketch. Tom Hanks is a good actor. He knew (we should) keep our mouths shut, keep our arms down. You don’t want to hold them up for the whole seven minutes of the cold open.

Moynihan said they probably would have figured all of this out before dress rehearsal, but they actually weren't paying much attention to the larger sketch. Instead, they spent like an hour talking about how absolutely absurd they felt being back in the costumes David S Pumpkins and the Skeletons, who have their own wild names. None of them ever thought the original sketch was going to hit, let alone lead to a TV special and an anniversary sketch a decade later.

You can watch the sketch in its entirety below…

That’s the power of SNL though. Some of the sketches that go viral and live on in people’s memories involve sharp political commentary or really thoughtful parodies of society. Others just involve a goofy character or characters that connect with people for whatever reason. David S Pumpkins and the Skeletons are definitely examples of those characters. They’re just so over the top and ridiculous that you can’t look away, even if they’re frozen in the background of a President Trump sketch and trying to stay as still as possible.

#3682. Blizzard adjusts popular World of Warcraft: Forever Battleground to stop players power-grinding rewards

"The overall intent for all of these changes was for games to feel more meaningful."

Many World of Warcraft: Forever players are currently in the midst of a substantial PvP reputation grind. However, this process has been disrupted due to a sudden change to one of the game's battleground PvP arenas.

The battleground in question is Alterac Valley, a 40 person-a-side clash between Alliance and Horde factions, where both sides need to push their forces across a snowy, mountainous map into the opposing faction's base to take down the NPC General waiting there. Alterac Valley is being grinded by max-level players for its gear rewards that are given once reaching "exalted" reputation there. Currently it's some of the best gear available ahead of raids being introduced next month.

Played the intended way, Alterac Valley is a lengthy battle. The Generals on both sides are fearsomely tough but by rushing to capture certain structures on the way to this battle, you can weaken the Generals enough to make them easier to overcome. As such, players have been fast-tracking this PvP instance, skipping smaller objectives and rushing core objectives to get to the Generals as fast as possible. This bypassed a lot of the incidental skirmishing allure of Alterac Valley, but it was an efficient way to quickly gain reputation and Honor points (PvP currency).

But this strategy has been pretty much killed outright as of today. In a post made to the official World of Warcraft forums, community manager Kaivax revealed that the reputation gained from killing the Generals has been drastically reduced, while the reputation gained from killing other NPCs and capturing previously ignored objectives now grants more. Generals are also granted a buff that makes them incredibly strong for the first 20 minutes of a match, which is then reduced for each objective taken.

This is a good change in regard to the experience of playing Alterac Valley. While rushing through was good for players looking to gain reputation quickly, they weren't really playing the Battleground in the way it's meant to be played. The dev post reads: "The overall intent for all of these changes was for games to feel more meaningful while trying to maintain a similar amount of rep gained over a similar playtime within the battleground, even with longer match lengths. There will be fluctuations depending on how successful you are at destroying towers and holding capture points at the end of a match however."

So how has the community reacted? Badly! Taking a gander at community hubs following this change shows plenty of frustration. Take this comment by Reddit user Athrek: "I'm fine with the changes if they give it Rank Points and calendar events. But they've gutted the rep for both sides, extended the time it takes to play, and it still gives zero Rank Points. Now you may as well get to the win condition and then sit there for a few hours, gaining the passive rep cause there's nothing else of value to be had."

It appears as of writing that the reputation gained isn't as much as it was previously, so those playing purely for reputation have been hit. There's another element of frustration which is that those who rushed to level 60 and ground Alterac Valley reputation and rewards before the changes won't be affected by this. Perhaps that's the allure of rushing to level 60!

"This is why the WoW mantra is 'exploit early, exploit often'," writes user Lanienah12. "Some people are already exalted with AV rep and will receive no punishment for it; meanwhile new people will be spending 3x as long." Especially in the wake of the Blackmaw Hold gold exploit being discovered by these frontrunners, there's a growing belief that those taking their time or that are limited by real-life factors are feeling the brunt of these changes.

If you replayed The Witcher 3 in its shiny new remastered form and got absolutely bodied by a couple of werewolf fights you thought were easier back when you had more youthful reflexes, don't worry—the problem wasn't your aging brain and hands after all. It was a bug that's been caught and exterminated in patch 5.02. "Fixed an issue where werewolves could regenerate health too quickly on higher difficulty settings," the patch notes say, "making them impossible to defeat."

Another problem some players had with The Witcher 3 Remastered was its lighting, with interiors in particular looking too dark while some other locations were washed-out flashbangs. Good news: "Fixed various lighting issues across multiple locations and cutscenes," the patch notes say, "including overly bright or dark areas, inconsistent lighting transitions and flickering." They've also "Fixed various lighting issues with hair when Path Tracing is enabled" and "Made various Path Tracing and Ray Reconstruction optimizations and visual improvements, including lighting, shadows, and water rendering."

That's all positive stuff, but the balance changes to various signs and mutations will be more controversial. The Remastered version launched with buffs to Witcher signs that made them useful even if you didn't specialize in them, but it may have overdone things a little. This patch walks back some of the potential for you to dominate the entire game with an Aard build, though changes like reducing the Catalyst skill's bonus to Aard and Igni intensity by 10% don't seem like they'll totally change the way you play.

I get that people don't like skill nerfs in singleplayer games, but I can also see CD Projekt anticipating next year's Songs of the Past DLC. They don't want to hear a bunch of players say, "It sucked because I trivialized the whole thing with a broken build I got by copying a YouTuber." If some skill nerfs and a reduction to stamina regeneration in combat mean you have to drink more potions to get your signs off, it probably won't ruin your fun.

Oh, and if you couldn't complete your Gwent collection because Zoltan Chivay's card didn't show up, the patch notes say it'll now appear in the correct place under the Hanged Man's Tree in Velen. Time to go back and get that 100% achievement at last.

#3680. Ubisoft reportedly goes all in on company-wide generative-AI use, and if developers don't want to use it, they have to explain why in detail

Ubisoft is clearly serious about implementing generative-AI deeply into the game development process. The French publisher now expects teams pitching new project ideas to be prepared to explain how gen-AI will help with developing the game.Teams who don't want to use gen-AI will need to clearly justify their reasoning to the higher-ups.

That's according to a new Vertical Slice report, citing multiple anonymous sources currently working at Ubisoft.

Several employees said that pitching a game idea without gen-AI or without explaining why it does not involve the use of the controversial tech will not receive the greenlight. This is especially relevant for smaller games with tight teams who now reportedly must deal with Ubisoft leaders' desire to implement gen-AI if they want to get their pitches reviewed.

"We were told that using AI will increase the speed at which pitches can be made by 'small lean agile teams,'" one source said. "We were told that as the goal was to move fast, iterate and discard projects to sift out the good stuff. AI was essential in maintaining a rapid pace."

While some said Ubisoft is not openly mandating gen-AI use to staff, others feel "cornered" by gen-AI. One source said Ubisoft views the tech as "unavoidable", and that only a minority of the company's audience reject it.

Ubisoft recently gave name to an internal initiative to expand the use of generative-AI and research how its developers can make use of the technology. It's called Motherbrain, and it has its own division within Ubisoft.

Over a year ago, Ubisoft embarked on a major restructuring effort that has seen the formation of new subsidiaries, the consolidation of its biggest brands into 'creative houses', the closure of studios and, of course, multiple rounds of layoffs.

"Ubisoft is in a top-down nightmare of AI psychosis," one source added, pointing to the already low morale within the company. "Yves [Guillemot] has hitched his wagon to the tech, demanding the rest of the company follow on."

#3677. Fed up of Steam's lack of action regarding AI slop? Maybe you should take a look at the 'Games Without AI' event, instead

Yesterday, a new Steam event went live that claims all games featured in it have avoided AI entirely during development. The event, called 'Games Without AI', has been set up by a third party rather than Valve - by Dev Land Marketing, All Ages Of Geek, and Dark Cocooning - to "support real creators" and runs from 25th November to 6th December.

"Behind every game, there are people, ideas, passion, and countless hours of creative work," said a mission statement. "We've carefully curated a selection of independent games that celebrate human creativity, craftsmanship, and collaboration, all made without generative AI. But Games Without AI is more than a festival. It's also about bringing developers, players, and creators together to build a community where we share knowledge, support one another, and grow together."

There are plenty of games featured in the event, and not just ones tied to the organisers, as the cynical-minded amongst you may expect. Ones that jump out to my eye are: Pidgeon Pocket, a 'cozy incremental' with pixel art and a flock of adorable pigeons that you need to upgrade; Bottled by Bears, which tasks you with collecting and discovering rare bees, bottling honey jars, and expanding your farm; and Arctic Awakening, which sort-of looks like Pacific Drive meets Subnautica, in the Arctic.

The event was posted to Reddit where commenters immidiately began accusing certain games of having used AI in their development - often without proof. One user, however, who claims to have been a developer trying to submit a game for inclusion in the event, offered some insight on how the selection process worked.

"As one of participants I can assure you that the qualification process was restrictive[ly] hard to bypass," they wrote. "We were all required to provide proofs of the game being made without AI and share as much of the process as possible. Then it was actually voted by community, which games are convicing enough so the whole process was intended to be as objective as possible. It's an event meant for developers who take pride in their games being made by humans so if any participant attends with ill intend of showing that AI generated game can get through... That would be very sad and shameful. From what I've seen, none of the selected games can be reasonable suspected of that. I also know some other participants personally and they are genuine zero-AI devs."

It's refreshing to see curation turned towards explicitly anti-AI games: between major publishers chasing the trend and smaller indie studios being caught out using the dubious tech, it's nice to see a library of games that promises that no AI was used during development. Given that Valve itself recently claimed it was up to developers themselves to ensure their games couldn't be ripped off by cheap AI tools, I'm happy to see an initiative rallying against the normalcy of all this.

The most recent Steam Next Fest had more than double the number of demos than last year, but that stat isn't what it seems on the surface: roughly 17 percent of those games listed the use of generative AI, but it seemed that many more games did not disclose the use of AI in their development. In June's event, more than a thousand games in Steam Next Fest featured a generative AI disclosure of some kind, which made up roughly 20 percent of all featured games.

Over the past 18 months or so, we've seen the issue of generative AI in games on Steam evolve quite a lot. AI tools have been used to clone games, resulting in a troubling trend of imitation games taking the spotlight away from real indie devs. Whilst Steam, as a storefront, has been steadfast in requiring games to declare their use of generative AI during development, there are loopholes: devs that claim they only use AI tools for "efficiency gains" can appear on the store without any declaration.

At the other end of the spectrum is Epic Games' Tim Sweeney, who last year criticised Valve's requirement to disclose generative AI, saying, "Steam and all digital marketplaces need to drop the 'Made with AI' label. It doesn't matter any more." The swell of users rejecting AI in games, though, seems to run counter to that argument. Recently, Big Walk developer House House revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" during the development of the co-op darling, and received a lot of backlash online.

#3676. Team Ninja Is Using AI For Quality Assurance, But Insists Creative Choices ‘Must Be Done By Humans’

Team Ninja is known, in part, for developing difficult games, but producers Kohei Shibata and Masakazu Hirayama emphasized during an interview with INVEN Global at GCON 2026 in South Korea that thereâs a key difference between difficult and unfair. The pair also spoke about how the Koei Tecmo subsidiary approaches the use of AI in games development, and an awkward compromise between implementing the technology for repetitive QA tasks, while arguing that “what matters fundamentally is that a game becomes fun when crafted by human hands.”

Shibata and Hirayama are best known for their work as producers on the Nioh and Wo Long series respectively, two games that take the combat-driven difficulty of the iconic Ninja Gaiden franchise and transpose it onto the world of samurai and Chinese mythology. Before the topic of AI arose, the two discussed the crucial role of player interaction and movement in their games, beginning with the similarities between all three franchises and most notably their swordplay and the focus on timing your attacks and reading an opponentâs next move. According to both, this process of requiring a player to learn an enemyâs next move and counter is key to straddling the line between challenging and frustrating play.

âI consider Nioh to be samurai action,â explained Shibata. âSamurai combat involves stillness and movement. You stand firmly grounded, observing the opponent’s moves, and deliver a sharp strike the instant an opening appears.â Meanwhile, for Hirayama on Wo Long, that game was defined by âaggressive Chinese martial arts action,â where âattack and defense flow together seamlesslyâ and where âaggressively attacking is important, but defense must also lead directly into the next attack.â

The two go on to argue that it’s important to make a game that is polished in a way that reduces friction between a player’s action and consequence. If a person fails, it must be their fault, not the game’s. âI believe [the core essence of action games is] control responsiveness,â Shibata explained. âWhen a player presses a button, the character must move exactly as they intended. If you press a button and the character doesn’t react properly, it causes frustration. Conversely, if a slight input causes an exaggerated movement, it feels awkward. Therefore, responsiveness to input must be simple and intuitive, and the movement must be communicated rapidly.â

We have seen numerous studios speak out in recent times about where they will and wonât use AI. While some Japanese developers are embracing the technology, others are more cautious, either avoiding it entirely or insisting they only use the technology for optimizing their development framework while leaving creative choices to humans. The latter is the direction being taken by Capcom with its next generation of RE Engine, and appears to also be the choice being made by Team Ninja, who are already using AI for QA purposes.

As Shibata explained, âCurrently, we utilize AI in QA and various verification tasks to streamline certain workflows. If we can use AI to shorten task times, we can dedicate that saved time toward elevating the game’s overall quality. In that sense, using AI is beneficial. However, since it is still a new technology, we are continuously evaluating the most appropriate ways to implement it. I imagine other game companies are facing similar questions.” He continued,

What matters fundamentally is that a game becomes fun when crafted by human hands. Repetitive, simple tasks that anyone must perform can be streamlined using technology. But ultimately, deciding how to craft the game and what makes it enjoyable must be done by humans. Using AI itself should never become the goal. I believe the principle that humans must think for themselves and finish the game will remain unchanged in the future.

Where, if anywhere, is an acceptable use of AI is a topic that remains up for debate, but it appears many developers are settling into a space where it is used to handle repetitive tasks. The use of AI in QA actually predates the modern conversations of generative AI, and doesnât necessarily rely on the tech: Sony, for instance, has been experimenting with AI for many years to test games. Whether this is something audiences are willing to tolerate, or indeed is something that will further threaten jobs in the games industry, remains to be seen.

Between Robert De Niro and Blythe Danner and Dustin Hoffman and Barbra Streisand, the Meet the Parents franchise has set a precedent for iconic parent casting. Now, following the release of Focker In-Law on the 2026 movie schedule, it seems like we could meet the parents of Ariana Grande’s Olivia at some point. So, with the final lines of the movie setting that up, I had to ask the cast and director about who could possibly play her mom and dad.

In Focker In-Law, after Olivia and Ben Stiller’s Greg clear the air and figure everything out, she notes that it’s time to meet her parents. And considering Focker In-Law is the fourth Focker film, I figured it’d only be natural if we got a Meet the Fockers-like sequel but with Olivia’s family.

So, when I interviewed the actors who play Ben Stiller’s kids (and son-in-law) in Focker In-Law, I had to ask who could play Grande’s parents. Beanie Feldstein, who plays Samantha, had a great idea for Olivia’s mom, saying:

I have one for her mom, which is Bernadette Peters. I really think that hits. That hits strong.

Now, moving on to her dad. Skyler Gisondo, who plays Henry (and Olivia’s fiancé by the end of the film), had a pretty wild idea for who could play that part, as he said:

What if Ben put on like this total prosthetic and did just old school play like seven characters.

I know he’s joking, but the idea of Ben Stiller doing what Mike Myers does in Austin Powers and playing a bunch of different characters would be hilarious.

Anyway, getting back to slightly more realistic answers, Eduardo Franco, who plays Samantha’s partner Eduardo in the movie, said Grande’s dad needs to be a “funny dude.” He also said:

I'm trying to think, man. It's gonna be funny. It's funny, dude. It's gotta be also probably into like singing and dancing and stuff. I'm trying to think.

Feldstein went on to note that “Olivia doesn’t sing or dance.” However, Franco lovingly said Grande does – as we all well know from her remarkable career as a pop star and her amazing work in the Wicked movies, which you can stream with a Disney+ subscription. So, whoever plays her dad has “got to be capable of what Ari can do.”

After that, the interview moved on, but toward the end of it, Franco finally came up with an idea for who could play Grande’s dad and blurted:

Javier Bardem. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Sorry. This whole time I've been. I'm so sorry. I've been thinking. He's Spanish, Español, but I mean, he'd be just as intimidating.

You know what? I see the vision. Javier Bardem could totally go toe to toe with Robert De Niro’s Jack. Plus, the idea of Ben Stiller’s Greg trying to keep up with him is already making me laugh.

Now, when I asked John Hamburg, the writer and director of Focker In-Law, this question about Grande’s parents, he was far more tight-lipped. He wouldn’t give me any clues, but he did say there have been conversations about it:

OK, I love CinemaBlend, and there's no way I'm going to share that information with you. I do have some people swirling around, and we even talked on set, you know, with Ben and Ari and Bob about who could possibly play her parents. But listen, I'm just trying to get through the release of this movie, OK? So I can't share yet.

Considering the movie ends on a big tease about who Olivia’s parents could be, I certainly hope we get an answer someday. However, for now, I’m just happy they’re all thinking about it.

So, while we wait to see if we get to Meet the Joneses, I’ll be picturing Javier Bardem and Bernadette Peters as Ariana Grande’s parents and hoping that the cast’s ideas actually pan out.

#3672. After playing the game, 30% of polled GTA 6 players want to buy flowers for a loved one, 9% accidentally punched cats

A new survey of Grand Theft Auto 6 players has found some particularly interesting results. 30 percent came away from the game with the desire to buy someone special flowers. Nine percent punched cats.

Per Games User Research's director Steve Bromley, 303 players from across the UK and US were polled on their experiences. They had to have at least two hours of playtime to contribute, which led to an informed sample of how folks are finding the game.

Those polled gave the game an 8.4/10 (that's 4.2/5 Eurogamer readers), which is glowing praise. 42 percent loved the narrative, as well as Jason and Lucia's relationship. 38 dug the lifelike and believable world, while 35 percent were keen on the freedom to explore and the variety of activities.

As for what they didn't like, 28 percent weren't a fan of the slow pacing and long cutscenes, 19 percent didn't like the difficulty in stealing cars and losing a wanted level, while 18 percent were put off by the game's technical performance.

Now for some fun findings: 41 percent expressed an interest in improving their real life after playing the game, with 30 percent of those looking to buy a loved one some flowers. Nice! 14 percent were at least once confused or stuck, due to confusion with the stealth, identifying time-sensitive missions, or experiencing control issues.

There's some bad news for the cats out there, too. Nine percent accidentally punched a cat while trying to pet it, while 61 percent had the same experience with human NPCs. At least it wasn't intentional, that has to count for something. Right?

#3671. Metal Slug Is The Latest Game From SNK In Line For A Movie Adaptation

The Saudi Arabian investment group is struggling to turn a profit from its investment in renowned Japanese developer SNK, as the 48-year-old company faces heavy losses following lower than expected sales. However, it might have have found a new medium through which to claw back its cash: the movies. Amidst Saudi Arabiaâs many other investments is new film studio The Arena, which has just announced Metal Slug as the latest property from the game studio to be in the works for a movie adaptation.

First reported by Variety, the studio announced that the adaptation of the side-scrolling military action platformer is going ahead, withÂ I Love My Dad director James Morosini attached to the project. An initial plot loosely based on the already thin narrative of theÂ Metal Slug series has also been revealed, centered on a misfit quartet of army recruits known as Marco Rossi, Tarma Roving, Eri Kasamoto and Fio Germi, as they stand up to General Morden to save the world from evil. Which seems about as coherent as a movie based on a game where soldiers fight aliens, yetis and zombies can get.

The Arena, originally revealed last year as Arena SNK Studios, is headed up by Erik Feig, a veteran producer who helped bring the likes of Twilight and La La Land to the screen. It was formed with backing from Saudi Arabiaâs Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and so far all of its projects bar one have been licensed from the SNK library. Currently in production is a webtoon called The Art of Fighting, and a TV series and movie based on Fatal Fury. It’s also working on a movie tied to Samurai Spirits, another SNK property. Their only non-SNK project is adapting a yet-to-be-released novel known as Kill Current.

Since its unveiling, the Arena’s only tangible output has been selling SNK fashion merchandise and running an Instagram account that seems to post about almost anything except its actual movies. Still, perhaps these movies and the occasional clothing merchandising drop are where investors hope to make back their money on buying SNK. Metal Slug at least has a concept lending itself to a more typical action blockbuster, but the question remains, with most of the studioâs IP resonating more with older audiences, can they turn these SNK IPs into something with mass appeal?

#3670. We are already in a world where people think about promoting games as human-made, Citizen Sleeper creator says

Citizen Sleeper creator Gareth Damian Martin - also known by their studio name Jump Over the Age - believes we're reaching a point of gen-AI saturation whereby game-makers are starting to counter-promote games as being human-made.

"We already are. Yeah, yeah, yeah. 100 percent," Damian Martin told me in an interview, while discussing their striking new game Signet City. "That was already something that my publisher [Fellow Traveller] was saying they want to do with my games more, especially with me doing the art this time as well. Yeah, 100 percent - it's going to give rise to that."

It's a label I haven't seen circulating in games yet, but we have seen an increase in the number of AI disclosures for games being sold on Steam, and many videos on YouTube now carry 'No AI' badges, in an effort to stand out from the torrent of videos made using gen-AI. We are already seeing Steam events dedicated to games without any AI usage whatsoever. Things are clearly changing.

Damian Martin told me "the only good thing" that could come from gen-AI use is a bounce-back effect of people noticing and cherishing human-made things more. They were reminded of this while looking at a Rembrandt sketch while doing a brief stint in art school ahead of Signet City (the art in the Citizen Sleeper games was commissioned, but the art in Signet City is done by them). In the sketch, the faces had been scribbled out, presumably because Rembrandt didn't like the work he'd done. They were scribbles that revealed the humanity of the creator.

"You suddenly remember that trying to represent a human face by using a pencil and a piece of paper is something that's been happening for hundreds of years," Damian Martin said. "So when you do it, you're connecting to an entire history of that challenge and that opportunity, and it's fascinating to me to engage and be part of that. It's really beautiful.

"If AI makes us notice that more," they added, "then I think that's great. If we can make a counter-punch, if we can find that energy, that's great. I certainly think if it gives value to human-made things, in a way that perhaps we'd been forgetting, then that's the only good thing that can come from that process."

To be clear, Damian Martin is not using gen-AI in making Signet City, a game about being a parasite in people's heads in a fictional version of Newcastle in the 1980s and then influencing what they do. It's a game with a distinct hand-drawn look, presented in a thick-lined, moody black-and-white way, and with bleak industrial backgrounds and post-punk influences and energy. Indeed, the idea Damian Martin would use gen-AI in any way runs counter and contrary to what they're known for.

"I exist in this space where the idea that I would use AI is kind of mad," they said. "It's a bit like me saying, 'I'm going to start buying all of my art materials from the asset store on Unity.' The reason people buy my games is because they come from me, and the only evidence I have - the only thing I can trust - is my own expression and identity. That's the thing that's worked for me; there's no other judgeable thing. So I'm working to put more of that into my games.

"But there is a real threat," they added, "and the reason there is a real threat in the wider games industry is because it's an industry, and people who work on games for big companies, in my experience, are treated very poorly. They are not respected as human beings in a lot of cases. So why would they not be replaced by machines if the people who pay their wages do not even respect their human nature? They do not respect their creativity. We've seen such a lack of respect for expression, for directors, for individuals within games."

"When something is industrial production and it doesn't care about the people involved, then it doesn't care whether they're machines or they're people as long as the work happens, and that's the real threat," they reiterated. "So we do have to be vigilant, and we do have to be loud and say stuff, and say that it's not okay for us, because otherwise it will happen. It just seems inevitable that you would try to automate these things because it's easier than having employees; that's the kind of horrible logic of industry, unfortunately. But that doesn't really concern me because I'm operating in a completely different mode."

Signet City currently has no release date but was said to be halfway through development when announced this summer. Citizen Sleeper 2 - Damian Martin's most recent game - was released at the beginning of 2025. It's a sequel that introduced more pressure into the heartwarming sci-fi, dice-rolling, role-playing series, and I thought it better for it. "With a new found sense of tension, and showpiece Contract missions, Citizen Sleeper is transformed. This follow-up has improved the RPG formula in every way," I wrote in my Citizen Sleeper 2 review.

The Wicker cast has been feeding into innuendo pretty much since all the horny reviews dropped for the 2026 movie release. Having seen the movie in theaters myself, I have to say I wholeheartedly approve. So, I guess I shouldn’t have been surprised when lead Olivia Colman pulled a wicker, penis-shaped vibrator out of her purse during a recent appearance, but I was! I wonder if Alexander Skarsgård knows she has this homage to his member on her person at any given time?

Wicker’s been landing some Oscar buzz, particularly in its Craft categories, but the leads have been out and about helping with the push in recent days. Lead Olivia Colman was recently out supporting Wicker when she signed on for British Vogue’s “What’s in my Bag” segment, which nearly always features an interesting array of random objects. In this case, one of the first things the actress pulled out was a Wicker vibrator, no joke.

She said fans might be “surprised” she’s just carrying around the wicker contraption, and joked she's “going to say it’s a lipstick" before also pulling out some Kitkats and Twix bars. See the surprise moment, below.

A post shared by British Vogue (@britishvogue)

I certainly didn’t see the wicker vibrator coming, but I do have questions. Namely, that doesn’t look like the very uncomfortable prosthetics Alexander Skarsgård was wearing on set. So, like where does one get a wicker vibrator? Did a fan make that and give it to her? Does she keep that in her bag all the time, or was this just tossed in to throw Wicker into the conversation? Again, does her co-star know she's carrying this around?

Any way you look at this, it's very funny, and as she succinctly put it:

If you’re offended by what I have in my bag, I don’t care.

With a Wicker Oscars push, anything is possible. Honestly I'd be down for some Best Actor/Actress noms. Colman and Skarsgård are so good in the movie and when I saw it in a theater full of women, the crowd was rowdy and having fun with the premise, which was so cheeky and unexpected. Even the merch for this movie follows suit! I mean, the popcorn bucket needs its own intimacy coordinator!

Anyway, I had the best time watching this movie, and I’ve totally enjoyed the way the two actors have been promoting the film in the time since, which includes but is not limited to Skarsgård’s feet (likely) ending up on wikifeet. This is the movie that really just keeps on giving and giving, and it just hit VOD so you can now even watch it from the comfort of your own home. I suggest you do so before awards season!

#3666. Rockstar Games employees vote against union recognition

Rockstar Games employees have voted against official recognition of the Rockstar Game Workers Union, with 93.2 percent of staff participating in the vote.

25 percent of those who participated voted to recognise the union, while 75 percent voted against. If it had been approved, it would have been the largest recognised union in the UK video game industry by a large margin. While the union will still exist and organise, Rockstar Games will not have to recognise the union as a representing body for staff at the studio, and is not obligated to attend regular meetings with the body.

Jennifer Kolbe, head of publishing at Rockstar Games told Eurogamer: "We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we've built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6. This result reflects our team's strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we're excited to build on all we've accomplished together."

The Rockstar Union also released a statement following the outcome of this vote, saying Rockstar employees will continue to organise despite the lack of recognition. It reads:

"For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn't a sign to retreat, it's a sign to double down on what we stand for. Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We're ready to put in the effort to make that happen.

"Whilst we haven't emerged with a recognition deal, this ballot has put our union on the radar of every worker, and opened the door for new kinds of conversation to start happening. People entirely unfamiliar with unions were for the first time debating employment conditions, collective bargaining rights, and our contracts. We heard from many more colleagues about what mattered to them, and we hope people will continue to engage so that we can see where these new discussions can lead us.

"A recognition agreement would have marked a path towards greater workplace democracy. But it's one route of many. At Rockstar we have already won, and will continue to win, tangible changes that improve our everyday lives. We'll keep fighting for a say. For pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against Al and layoffs.

"The power to shape our working lives has always been, and will always be, in our hands."

Rockstar employees represented by the union are still awaiting the verdict from the Rockstar Games vs IWGB employment tribunal legal case, of which the final verdict is still pending. This case was kicked off by the sudden firing of employees present in a union Discord server. The employees claim this was an attempt at union busting by Rockstar, while the company denies this, saying it was for breaking confidentiality agreements.

It's hard to imagine Christmas without Buddy the Elf, but Hollywood wasn't convinced the movie would work.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With the holiday season upon us and the 2026 movie calendar winding down, there are a handful of the best Christmas movies I return to every December, and Elf is pretty much guaranteed to make the list. Will Ferrell running around New York City in yellow tights, eating spaghetti covered in candy and screaming about Santa Claus has become as much a part of the holidays as putting up the tree. According to one of the movie's stars, Hollywood wasn't exactly convinced it had a future Christmas classic on its hands back in 2003.

Andy Richter, who played Morris in the Jon Favreau-directed comedy, recently reflected on the making of Elf and explained why the movie was considered something of a gamble. Speaking with People while promoting his new book, Elf: Unwrapped, which he co-wrote with Aaron Karo, Richter said the movie's eventual success makes it easy to forget just how uncertain things were when production began.

It was a risky movie, and nobody thinks about that because it’s now a classic, but at the time there was nobody that was aching to make a movie with Will Ferrell as the star or with Jon Favreau as the director, for that matter.

Considering Will Ferrell himself had doubts when he first tried on Buddy's iconic costume, I can understand why some studio executives might have been nervous. At the time, the SNL alum was best known for his work on Saturday Night Live, where he'd spent seven seasons establishing himself as one of the show's biggest stars. He'd appeared in movies like Old School and Zoolander, but he hadn't yet proven he could carry a major studio comedy as its leading man.

Favreau, meanwhile, had directed the 2001 comedy Made, but he was still relatively inexperienced behind the camera. According to Richter, the studio was taking a chance on both men. He added:

They were rolling the dice with this movie and it really paid off.

It's funny to think about now, considering Ferrell went on to become one of the biggest comedy stars of the 2000s, while Favreau would eventually direct Iron Man, helping launch the Marvel Cinematic Universe. He's also had a major hand in shaping the modern Star Wars franchise with The Mandalorian. But back in 2003, the idea of giving a relatively untested leading man a Christmas comedy about a grown man raised by elves probably sounded pretty ridiculous on paper. And considering some of the behind-the-scenes stories about making Elf, it's remarkable how well everything came together. It is a ridiculous premise. That's a big part of why I love it.

Richter also credited the combination of Ferrell's comedic instincts and Favreau's approach to storytelling for making the movie work. Interestingly, though, the movie’s star recently addressed the longstanding rumors about his relationship with Favreau during the production. It seems there's still plenty to learn about what went into making this particular Christmas classic. As for Richter, he told the outlet that the film succeeds because:

The combination of their two sensibilities, which we go into in the book, that really made it work because it’s funny, but also has a lot of heart.

I think that's a pretty accurate assessment. Ferrell gets to be completely absurd as Buddy, whether he's congratulating a coffee shop for having the world's best cup of coffee or trying to navigate a revolving door. Yet the movie also gives us a genuinely sweet story about a guy looking for his father and trying to find somewhere he belongs.

James Caan's performance as Walter Hobbs deserves some credit here, too. His perpetually irritated reaction to Buddy's enthusiasm makes their relationship work, and without that dynamic, I don't think the movie would have nearly the same emotional payoff. Whatever reservations Hollywood had about the project, audiences certainly didn't share them once it arrived in theaters.

According to The Numbers, Elf opened to more than $31 million during its first weekend in November 2003. It has since earned approximately $234 million worldwide, including revenue from subsequent theatrical releases. That's a pretty impressive return for a movie with a reported $32 million production budget.

The movie was successful enough that Hollywood naturally wanted another one, though Ferrell has since explained why he walked away from a potentially lucrative Elf sequel.

More than two decades later, it's difficult to imagine the holiday season without Buddy the Elf. The movie remains a favorite among families, and people are still finding new things to appreciate about it, including one particularly interesting question about Buddy's journey from the North Pole to New York City.

I find it interesting that a movie nobody could guarantee would succeed has become something people practically schedule their Christmas celebrations around. Ferrell has made plenty of successful comedies since, and Favreau's career has gone places nobody could have predicted in 2003.

There's something special about Elf. Considering how many Christmas movies come and go without making much of an impression, I suspect the people who took that gamble are pretty happy they did.

Elf is streaming with a Hulu subscription.
